findings.criterion: (2) onboarding brings up a working, secure-by-default instance with zero manual token handling
findings.message: Phase 3's 'One-shot out-of-band token bootstrap' specifies opening the browser exactly once. However, the Phase 3 exposure matrix explicitly supports SSH tunnels and Tailscale, which implies the instance may run on a remote headless server. On a headless machine, attempting to automatically launch a local browser will fail, entirely breaking the zero-manual-token-handling onboarding flow. The plan must account for remote/headless onboarding without violating the zero-manual-token requirement or regressing to manual token copy-pasting.

findings.criterion: (4) works-on-arrival cross-platform... with no manual git surgery
findings.message: Phase 4 claims the update path requires 'no manual git surgery,' but handles local edits by refusing the update with 'explicit stash/reset instructions.' Asking a collaborator to drop to the CLI, run git stash/reset, retry the update, and then manually reapply their stash over the new release is the definition of manual git surgery. If local edits are possible, either the update orchestrator must handle preservation and restoration automatically, or the 'no manual git surgery' claim is false under these conditions.

findings.criterion: (5) none of this regresses the durability... already has
findings.message: Phase 2's Windows durability contract handles rename contention by retrying for ~1s and then 'fails LOUDLY.' While failing loudly prevents torn writes, throwing an exception and dropping a write (or crashing the agent) simply because Windows Defender or Search locked a file for 1.5 seconds is a severe operational regression for Windows collaborators. The ~1s retry bound is often insufficient against Windows AV scanners, meaning the system's runtime resilience will degrade on NTFS.

The 'anchor update' walkthrough explicitly lists its steps (verify tag -> ff-only merge -> doctor -> capability diff) but entirely omits updating dependencies (e.g., 'npm install'). If release N+1 adds a new package dependency, the collaborator's instance will crash on boot because node_modules is out of date, violating the 'works-on-arrival' criterion for updates.

Moving the status block to an engine-emitted template and explicitly removing status-request text from agent prompts eliminates the LLM's subjective self-reporting. This strips the agent of its cognitive grounding (articulating its current state, blockers, and intent before acting), replacing it with mechanical logging and severely regressing the system's core 'honesty' engineering.

To pass the token in a client-side URL fragment during the out-of-band bootstrap, the system must spawn the OS's browser launcher (e.g., 'start', 'open', 'xdg-open') with the target URL. This injects the token directly into the argv of that child process, violating the proposed invariant that 'the token never appears on any process argv' and ensuring the CI test will fail.

The draft states skill hashes are 'verified at engine start'. If the engine dynamically reloads skill files from disk during a long-running session without re-verifying the hash at read time, a collaborator can bypass immutability by editing the file post-boot. Verification must occur at load/read time, not just boot time.

findings.criterion: (2) secure-by-default instance with zero manual token handling
findings.section: Phase 3 — Default-Deny Security Model and Zero-Friction Token
findings.message: The plan states 'the token never appears on any process argv' but simultaneously mandates that onboarding 'opens the browser exactly once with the token in the URL fragment'. Opening the default system browser with a specific URL intrinsically requires passing that URL on the browser process's command line (argv). This exposes the bootstrap token to any local process that can read process listings (e.g., via WMI/Task Manager on Windows, or `ps` on POSIX), making the core token-hygiene invariant structurally impossible to satisfy as designed.

findings.criterion: (3) safe to run and safe to expose
findings.section: Phase 7 — Release Integrity and External Red-Team Gate
findings.message: The plan states 'the onboard and update scripts verify tag signature and hash before install'. This is secure for updates where an existing trusted script verifies the incoming fetch, but it is structurally flawed for the initial onboard. If a collaborator clones the repository and runs the onboarding script from that untrusted clone, an attacker who compromised the repository could simply remove the verification logic from the script. The initial verification must be anchored externally, not by the code being verified.

findings.criterion: (3) safe to run and safe to expose
findings.section: Phase 3 — Default-Deny Security Model and Zero-Friction Token
findings.message: The exposure matrix relies on a 'token-derived session cookie on EVERY route' for the default loopback posture, but completely omits CSRF protections or `SameSite=Strict` cookie attributes. Because it binds to loopback, any malicious website the user visits in their browser can issue cross-site requests to 127.0.0.1. Without explicit CSRF tokens or strict SameSite enforcement, the application is vulnerable to ambient-authority attacks from the public web.
